newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mobutu backs multinational force for Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu backs multinational force for Zaire.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko told a U.N. envoy on Wednesday he supported proposals for a multinational force to get relief to refugees in his country and help them return home.

Envoy Raymond Chretien quoted Mobutu as saying he would do his utmost so that a unilateral ceasefire declared by Tutsi rebels fighting Zairean forces could hold in order to let the multinational force work.

"President Mobutu told me Zaire would do everything possible to maintain this period of calm so that the multinational force discussed in Nairobi may be able to rapidly allow for food to reach refugees and help them return to their home countries, including of course Rwanda," said Chretien.
"He was very clear, very categorical," the envoy told reporters after the half-hour meeting at Mobutu's French Riviera villa.
Zaire's ambassador to France, Baya Ramazani, was more defiant, telling reporters that Rwanda had intervened to back the Tutsi rebels who have seized the Zairean towns of Goma and Bukavu.
"(Zaire) cannot stay idle, just waiting for diplomatic efforts to succeed," he said.

An eight-nation African summit in Nairobi on Tuesday called on the United Nations to send a "neutral" protection force to create havens from which refugees could go home along safe corridors. But volunteers for the force appeared sparse.
France, Spain and Ethiopia have offered troops for the force, initially proposed by the French. Paris insists all major countries must participate and that African troops should rapidly take over.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette voiced frustration and accused the international community of being spineless.
"I'm knocking on doors, asking if anyone is prepared to assume his responsibilities. The answer is 'Could you come back tomorrow' or 'We might lend an aircraft'," he said in a television interview.
Chretien, Canada's ambassador to the United States, planned to fly later to Kinshasa for talks with Zairean Prime Minister Kendo wa Dondo, and to Kigali for talks with Rwanda officials.
He said he would remind Rwanda of a consensus among African countries that borders must not be called into question.
Chretien said he would also ask Kigali's views on how to handle the Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire who fled Rwanda in fear of reprisal for the 1994 massacres of Tutsis.
"Rwanda lived through absolutely terrible times a few years ago. It is entitled to demand some conditions for the return of the refugees," he said.
Chretien said he found Mobutu in good form and able to discuss all major issues.

The 66-year-old Zairean president, who has been away from Zaire since August undergoing treatment for prostate cancer, made a brief appearance before a handful of reporters at his palatial villa but did not talk to them.
Wearing an elegant black and white jacket but without his customary leopard skin hat, he looked thin and tired.
Ramazani said Mobutu was getting better and would return home in a few days. "The situation demands it," he said.
In Kinshasa, Mobutu's spokesman Samba Kabuya Lumuna said no one knew exactly when the president would return.

Mobutu underwent surgery for his cancer in Switzerland. He left Lausanne on Monday for his sprawling, pink and white marble villa near Nice. He has remained silent since fighting broke out in his country.
Ramazani said Mobutu was following developments back in Zaire through regular contacts with senior officials and all government actions were taken in agreement with him.
